text.what: A black grape from north-eastern France that ripens early, carries thin skin over tight pinecone-shaped bunches, and mutates more readily than almost any vine in cultivation. It gives pale wine with low tannin and high acid, and it rewards cold ground, which is why growers chase it toward the poles, the fog and the hills.
text.story: Pinot sits one or two generations from wild Vitis sylvestris, which makes it about as old as cultivated vines get. Crossed with the peasants' workhorse Gouais blanc somewhere in medieval north-eastern France, it fathered chardonnay, gamay, aligoté, auxerrois, melon and eleven more — half the vineyards of France descend from that one mismatch between the nobility's plot and the commoner's. *Tradition holds —* the dukes of Burgundy did the rest of the marketing.
text.how: Thin skins and little phenolic material give pale, medium-bodied, low-tannin wine. The same skins split and rot in a wet September. It buds early into frost, ripens early into heat, and its tight bunches trap moisture — every fault it has comes from the same anatomy that makes the wine taste the way it does.
text.today: Grown on every continent that can chill it: Burgundy and Champagne, Germany's Ahr and Baden, Oregon, California's fog corridors, Central Otago, Tasmania, Patagonia, the Cape.

text.what: A strip of limestone running south-west from Dijon where pinot noir and chardonnay have been sorted, fenced and argued over for a thousand years. Everything here is small: the hill is 40 km long and rarely 2 km wide, and it carries 100 appellations stacked in four ranks.
text.story: Medieval monks and the Valois dukes did the surveying: which parcel ripened, which drained, which froze. Denis Morelot wrote it down in 1831; Jules Lavalle classified it in 1855; the Beaune agricultural committee formalised it in 1861; and when the AOC laws arrived in 1936 most of Lavalle's first class became grands crus. The ranks on today's label are a nineteenth-century map given the force of law.
text.how: Four ranks, and the smaller the ground the louder the name. Grand cru takes 2% of production at 35 hl/ha and labels the vineyard alone. Premier cru takes 12% at 45 hl/ha and labels village plus vineyard. Village wines take 36% at 50 hl/ha across 42 villages. Regional Bourgogne carries the rest. A grower may always sell down a rank, never up.
text.today: UNESCO inscribed the climats in 2015, which put a heritage listing on a land-holding pattern rather than a building.

text.what: A funnel opening west to the Pacific at 34.9°N — further south than anywhere sensible for pinot noir, and colder through the growing season than most of Oregon. The transverse ranges turn this valley east-west, the ocean walks straight in, and summer averages 75°F.
text.story: Grapes grew here in the 1830s, under the Mexican land grants. Modern planting starts in 1964 with a hundred acres; by the mid-1970s there were over 2,000. The AVA came on 5 August 1981 — the country's third, California's second, and the first for either county. In 2010 the TTB pushed the southern line out to the watershed, adding 18,790 acres and nine vineyards.
text.how: Morning fog takes hours to burn off and afternoon wind replaces it. Winkler Region I. Under 14 inches of rain in a normal year, so nearly everything is irrigated.
text.today: Pinot noir and chardonnay are the appellation's two flagship varieties — and the same valley cooks the beef that made it famous, over oak cut off these hills.

text.what: Three and a half million acres of Oregon between the Coast Range and the Cascades, of which a thin band of hillside grows pinot noir. Eleven AVAs now sit inside it.
text.story: David Lett planted pinot noir at Dundee in 1965 against the advice of everyone at Davis, who said Oregon was too cold and too wet. Adelsheim chaired the committee that petitioned for the AVA in 1983.
text.how: Cool and wet, with rain that arrives near harvest and decides the vintage. Growers pick on the forecast as much as on sugar.
text.today: Pinot noir covered 24,729 acres of Oregon in 2022 and brought the highest price per ton of any variety in the state.

text.what: Eight hundred acres on the Santa Maria bench, planted in 1969 and farmed row by row for whoever buys the rows. Over 250 acres of it is pinot noir, and the vineyard's name appears on more labels than most wineries manage.
text.story: Tomás Olivera took the Rancho Tepusquet grant from Governor Alvarado in 1837; Chumash had fished Tepusquet Creek long before that. text.how: Blocks are sold by area rather than by the ton, so a winemaker who wants to crop hard is not arguing with a grower paid by weight. Some customers have bought the same rows for over twenty years and print the block on the label.
text.today: Also one of California's larger sources of certified budwood — a good deal of the state's chardonnay started as cuttings from here.

text.what: The wood the whole style rests on. In Santa Maria, red oak means coast live oak — Quercus agrifolia — which grows on the hills around the valley and burns down to hot, steady coals without throwing much smoke.
text.how: Split, burned down to coals in a firebox or at the edge of the pit, then raked under a grate on a hand crank. The cook moves the meat up and down instead of moving the fire. Little smoke matters here: the valley is windy, and the cooking is hot and quick rather than long and low.
text.notes: The local name turns out to be good botany. Coast live oak is a semi-evergreen oak of the California Floristic Province, growing from Mendocino south into northern Baja, and it sits in the red oak section of the genus — though unusually for that group its acorns ripen in seven or eight months rather than eighteen. Californio Spanish called the tree encina, which is why Encinitas and Encinal are on the map.

text.what: A triangular two-to-five-pound piece of bottom sirloin, rolled in salt, pepper and garlic, grilled over red oak coals to medium-rare and sliced across the grain. In its home valley it arrives with pinquito beans, salsa, green salad and buttered French bread grilled on the same fire.
text.story: The barbecue is older than the cut. Californio ranchers fed their vaqueros each spring from oak-coal pits, and the Santa Maria Club ran a stag barbecue for up to 700 people a month from 1931. Top sirloin was the meat. In the late 1950s a market manager in Santa Maria put a triangular piece that usually went to the grinder on a rotisserie instead, and by the 1960s the town had a cut of its own.
text.how: Grill directly over red oak, fat side up, turning once; pull at 130–135 °F and let it rest before slicing. The grain changes direction inside the muscle, so the knife has to change with it. Central California butchers leave the fat cap on; butchers elsewhere trim it.
text.today: Sold country-wide now, and still the default thing to cook at a Santa Maria Valley fundraiser, rodeo or school benefit.

sections.text: 27 CFR part 9 lists every American Viticultural Area, its boundary and the Federal Register notice that made it. It is a work of the United States government and free of copyright. This project harvested the whole part from the eCFR — 289 sections, 284 of them carrying a Federal Register year — and every AVA date on this site comes from there rather than from a repetition of it.

Country outlines, subdivisions and coastline come from Natural Earth, public domain. Cellar and tasting-room points come from OpenStreetMap under ODbL, harvested through Overpass inside named boxes — which is why the map is dense in Baden and empty in places that certainly have wineries. An empty box means nobody has tagged them, not that nobody is there.

Wikipedia articles are used as a corpus and cited by revision, so a citation points at the text this project actually read. They are CC BY-SA. Where a claim rests only on a Wikipedia article, the record says so; where it rests on general knowledge of the subject, the provenance tier says tradition and the sentence is hedged.

The books in the source list — the Oxford Companion, the World Atlas, Wine Grapes, Jasper Morris on Burgundy, Haeger on North American pinot noir — are in copyright and are cited, never quoted at length. Recipes are only reproduced where the licence allows it; otherwise this site lists ingredients, which are facts, and leaves the method to whoever wrote it.

No record carries a field observation yet. Planted area is missing for most single vineyards. Hours are missing for most cellars, and a missing day is shown as unknown rather than guessed. OpenStreetMap returned no winery at all inside the Anderson Valley box on 16 September 2026, which says something about tagging and nothing about Anderson Valley.

text.what: Burgundy spent a thousand years working out which slope did what. Everyone else has had about sixty years, and has spent most of it looking for the same three things: a cold growing season, a long one, and something in the ground that drains.

What made it portable at scale.
And the less official route.

sections.text: Pinot noir ripens early, which in a warm place means it ripens too fast: sugar arrives before flavour and the acid falls out. It has thin skin, which in a wet place means rot. It buds early, which in a frosty place means no crop. Every region that grows it well has found a way to be cold without being lethal — fog, altitude, a lake, a wind gap, a long maritime autumn.

David Lett left UC Davis in 1964 with a plan to grow pinot noir outside Burgundy and, in 1965, planted in the Willamette Valley against the advice of every professor he had. His 1975 South Block Reserve placed tenth in a Paris tasting in 1979. Robert Drouhin ran the comparison again in Beaune the next year, where it came second by a fraction to one of his own wines. In 1987 the Drouhin family bought land in the Dundee Hills.

California's answer was not altitude but marine air. Fog runs up the Russian River gap, through the Navarro at Anderson Valley, across the Carneros shoulder from San Pablo Bay, and straight into the transverse valleys of Santa Barbara County — where the mountains run east-west and let the ocean walk inland. Russian River pinot plantings went from about 4,000 acres to over 12,000 between the late 1990s and 2003. Santa Maria Valley, at 34.9°N, runs colder through the growing season than most of Oregon.

Central Otago planted 92 hectares and grew to 1,930, with over 80% of it pinot noir — the only region of its size to bet that hard on one variety. Martinborough took a gravel terrace in a rain shadow. Tasmania and Mornington took the sea. Chile took the Humboldt current, South Africa took the clay behind Hermanus, and Patagonia took wind and long light.

Cuttings, mostly, and arguments. Pommard and Wädenswil through UC Davis, then the Dijon numbers through the French selection programme and Oregon's importers. Some of it moved less formally: New Zealand still tells the story of a cutting confiscated at Auckland airport and handed to a customs officer who made wine. What did not travel is the part Burgundy spent a millennium on — a map of which parcel does what, drawn by people who had time to be wrong repeatedly.

sections.h: Why a vine needs a number
sections.text: Pinot noir mutates readily — there are hundreds of clones in vineyards and collections — and it carries virus. Leafroll and fanleaf will quietly cost a grower ripeness for thirty years. Clonal selection answers both: pick one vine that performs, test it clean, propagate it, give it a number, and every plant from that line behaves roughly the same.

France's national programme selected and certified pinot noir clones through the university and research station at Dijon, and the numbers — 113, 114, 115, 667, 777, 828 and others — reached the New World from the 1980s. *Tradition holds —* Raymond Bernard directed the work and helped get the first material to Oregon. Before that, American plantings ran mostly on Pommard (UCD 4) and Wädenswil (UCD 1A and 2A) out of UC Davis, and Oregon made its early reputation on exactly those two.

Uniformity. A block of one clone ripens together, which is convenient, and tastes like one thing, which is not always what you want. Growers hedge by planting several numbers in strips and blending them back, or by taking cuttings from an old block instead — massal selection, which keeps the variation and the virus together.

California also learned what happens when nobody checks: high-cropping upright selections sold as 'Gamay Beaujolais' were pinot noir under another name, and a generation of plantings suffered for it.

Certified material is slow. Quarantine and virus indexing take years, and growers in a hurry have always found other routes. The California trade repeats that the Calera selection came home with Josh Jensen from Burgundy; New Zealand tells the Abel story as folklore. Neither is documented, both are planted widely, and the nurseries that sell certified vines will tell you exactly what that costs everybody else.

A 2009 Sonoma State University study found the film slowed merlot's growth and pushed its price down, but concluded that its main effect was a rise in pinot noir's volume and price, and in wine consumption overall.

sections.h: What it did to a county
sections.text: The road trip runs through the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills, and the tasting rooms it passed got a decade of visitors out of it. *Inference —* the timing helped: the Sta. Rita Hills AVA had been established in 2001, so a region with a new name on the label got a national advertisement for free, three years in.

It did not teach anyone what pinot noir tastes like, and it did not change a single thing in a vineyard. The vines that carried the increase were already in the ground — planted by people who had spent the 1980s and 1990s being told the variety was a dead end.

kin.as: The vine in question.

sections.text: Thin skin splits in rain and rots in humidity. Tight bunches hold moisture against the berries and keep spray out. Early budding walks into spring frost; early ripening walks into a September heat spike that strips acid in days. Little pigment and little phenolic material mean the wine is pale and low in tannin whatever the grower does — so anything that would normally hide a fault has nowhere to hide it.

There is no ballast. Excess new oak shows. Brett shows. Over-extraction turns green rather than powerful, because there is not much tannin to draw and what there is comes with the bitter end of the skins and seeds. Most pinot cellar technique is about restraint and about texture: gentle cap work, old barrels, and decisions made in the first three days.

Low yields by rule and by habit, hand picking, sorting, small fermenters, more barrels per litre than a big red needs, and a variety that will refuse a vintage outright. That arithmetic is why grand cru Burgundy costs what it costs, and it is also why so much cheap pinot noir tastes hollow: the grape does not have a cheap register.

A triangle of beef, two to three pounds trimmed, rolled in salt, black pepper and garlic before it goes on. It cooks over oak coals on an iron grate that a hand crank raises and lowers, comes off at medium-rare, rests, and gets sliced thin across the grain. Beside it: pinquito beans, fresh salsa, a tossed green salad, and French bread split, dipped in melted butter and grilled on the same fire. Many local kitchens add Portuguese linguiça to the fire alongside the beef.

This is not the barbecue of a smoker and a long afternoon. The meat sits close to hot coals and cooks in under an hour. The fire does the seasoning that a sauce does elsewhere, and nothing gets mopped or glazed.

sections.h: The valley cooked before it grew grapes
sections.text:
The Santa Maria Valley opens west to the Pacific, which is the fact that explains everything else about it — the barbecue, the wine and the weather all follow from a valley that runs the wrong way. The Chumash were here first; Tepusquet Creek carries a Chumash name that means fishing for trout.

In 1837 Governor Juan Bautista Alvarado granted Tomás Olivera two square leagues as Rancho Tepusquet — nearly 9,000 acres running up to the San Rafael Mountains. Olivera sold to his stepdaughter María Martina Osuna and her husband Juan Pacífico Ontiveros in 1855; Ontiveros started an adobe in 1857 and raised horses, cattle, sheep, grain — and wine grapes.

The barbecue grows straight out of that economy. Californio ranchers fed their vaqueros each spring from pits of oak coals dug in the ground, and served pinquitos alongside. Local barbecue historian R. H. Tesene put the turn into style like this: residents began stringing cuts of beef on skewers or rods and cooking them over the coals of a red oak fire. In 1931 the Santa Maria Club started a monthly stag barbecue that drew up to 700 people at a sitting. The cut then was top block sirloin, rolled in salt, pepper and garlic salt — the same seasoning, on a different muscle.

sections.h: The fire, and the wood that stays home
sections.text:
Red oak here means coast live oak, Quercus agrifolia: a semi-evergreen tree of the California Floristic Province, growing from Mendocino down into northern Baja, and covering the hills around this valley. It does sit in the red oak section of the genus, so the local name is not the folk error people assume — though its acorns ripen in seven or eight months where most red oaks take eighteen. Californio Spanish called it encina; that is where Encinitas and Encinal come from.

What the wood does matters more than what it is called. It burns down to hot, dense coals and throws little smoke, which suits a hot, quick cook in a windy valley. The rig suits it too: a welded iron box, a grate on a hand crank, and a cook who controls temperature by winching meat up and down rather than by moving fire around.

And this is the part of the tradition that will not travel. A cut of beef ships anywhere. Salt, pepper and garlic are on every shelf. Beans can be posted. The tree cannot — so the further you get from the Central Coast, the more the same recipe becomes a marinade argument conducted over the wrong fuel.

sections.h: The cut, and the five men who claim it
sections.text:
Tri-tip is the tensor fasciae latae, the triangular muscle at the bottom of the sirloin. Untrimmed it runs around five pounds. American meat buyers know it as IMPS/NAMP 185C, bottom sirloin butt, tri-tip. Butchers in central California leave the fat cap on for the grill; butchers elsewhere cut it off to make the piece look tidier on a tray.

The claims, in order of the dates attached to them:

**1915.** The cut appears in American trade usage as 'the triangle part' of the loin butt. So the muscle was noticed long before anyone marketed it.

**Second World War.** Rondo Brough, an Army butcher working in southern California, said he made 'triangle tip' a cut of its own to get an extra portion out of the animal and cut down on scrap. Colleagues carried the idea into California shops and restaurants after the war.

**1950s, Oakland.** Otto Schaefer Sr. named and marketed tri-tip there.

**1950s, New York.** Butcher and restaurateur Jack Ubaldi said he named and sold the same cut as 'Newport steak'.

**1955, Long Beach.** Jack's Corsican Room served triangle tip cooked in wine.

**Late 1950s, Santa Maria.** Larry Viegas, a butcher at the Santa Maria Safeway, told it this way: the store had a glut of hamburger, his manager Bob Schutz took a piece of the unwanted triangle that would normally have been ground, seasoned it with salt, pepper and garlic salt, and put it on a rotisserie for three quarters of an hour or so. It went over well, and Schutz began selling it as tri-tip.

**1964, Palm Springs.** Desert Provisions advertised the cut under the name tri-tip.

So: Santa Maria did not invent the muscle, and probably did not coin the name on its own. What the valley did was marry the cut to a fire, a seasoning and a plate that were already a century old, and then keep doing it in public every weekend until the combination had a name. The rest of the world calls the same piece aiguillette baronne in France, Bürgermeisterstück or Pastorenstück in northern Germany, Hüferschwanz in Austria, rabillo de cadera in Spain, colita de cuadril in Argentina and maminha in Brazil — every one of them a name that treats it as a roast, not a steak.

sections.h: Who cooks it, and who says what it is
sections.text:
By the late 1950s four places were becoming the town's landmarks for this food: the Far Western Tavern, the Valley Steakhouse, the Hitching Post and Jocko's. Service-club pits still cook it at rodeos, school fundraisers and church benefits, which is where most people in the valley first eat it.

President Reagan liked it. Local pitmaster Bob Herdman and his Los Compadres crew cooked it for him repeatedly, including five times on the South Lawn of the White House.

The Santa Maria Valley Chamber of Commerce runs a Santa Maria Style Barbeque Association, which describes the tradition in the terms above — beef rolled in salt, pepper and garlic, cooked on skewers or rods over coals of red oak native to the valley — and points readers at certified locations. On 16 September 2026 its page invited places to get certified but did not publish the criteria. The trade also repeats that the Chamber registered the name and the menu in 1978; the Chamber's own post about that returned HTTP 403 to this project, so the claim is recorded here without a source this project has read.

sections.h: The same hills grow pinot noir
sections.text:
Commercial vines came back to this valley in 1964 — a hundred acres, planted by growers who thought the ground could rival Napa. By the mid-1970s there were over 2,000 acres. In 1969 the Miller family bought Rancho Tepusquet, reunited two pieces of the old grant, and planted what is now Bien Nacido: over 800 acres, more than 250 of them pinot noir, sold row by row to winemakers rather than by the ton.

On 5 August 1981 the Santa Maria Valley became an American Viticultural Area — the country's third, California's second, and the first for Santa Barbara or San Luis Obispo county. The TTB pushed the southern boundary out to the watershed line in 2010, adding 18,790 acres and nine vineyards, and taking the AVA to 116,273 acres.

The climate reads like an error. This is 34.9°N — the latitude of Los Angeles, of Beirut, of Casablanca — and the growing season is colder than most of the Willamette Valley. Morning fog takes hours to clear, afternoon wind replaces it, and summer averages 75°F: Winkler Region I, the coolest class the scale has. Rain runs under 14 inches in a normal year, so the vines drink from a pipe. Pinot noir and chardonnay are the appellation's flagship varieties.

Which means the barbecue and the wine come off the same slopes. Oak on the hillsides, vines on the bench below, beans on the valley floor, and a town in the middle that cooks all three.

sections.h: So what do you drink with it?
sections.text:
Start with what the food does, because the food is the harder half.

The meat is lean, with a fat cap on one side and a salty, charred crust on all of them. It is served medium-rare, so there is blood and iron in it. The salsa is sharp — raw tomato, chilli, onion, celery, vinegar — and it goes on top, not on the side. The beans are earthy and often carry pork. The bread is buttered and grilled. Nothing on the plate is sweet, and nothing is sauced in the barbecue-sauce sense.

Now what pinot noir brings: acid, modest tannin, red fruit, and — in wine from this valley in particular — a savoury, faintly bloody note that sits close to what rare beef already tastes like. *Inference —* the acid is the hinge. A sharp salsa flattens a soft, low-acid red and leaves it tasting of nothing; a wine with acid of its own meets it instead. Iron in rare meat and iron-edged savour in the wine are a match by similarity, which is the same reason duck works.

What cuts the other way, and it is a real objection: char and oak smoke are bullies. A delicate bottle can simply lose. Tri-tip is also lean enough to leave tannin unbuffered — there is little fat to soften it — which is an argument against a big tannic red as much as for a small one. *Inference —* the risk with pinot is not tannin, it is scale: a light village wine gets buried, while the denser Santa Maria bottles, with their stem spice and their savour, stand up.

What the valley itself pours is a separate question from what theory says, and the sources this project has read do not answer it. The tradition's own literature describes the plate in detail and says nothing about wine. Local steakhouses stock the county's syrah and cabernet as well as its pinot. **This page will not hand down a verdict it cannot source.** What it can say is that the two things came off one piece of ground, and that the ground's cold fog explains both of them.

Buy it with the fat cap on, or ask for it. Season heavily: the tradition is salt, black pepper and garlic — garlic salt in the old accounts — rolled over the whole piece.

Build a bed of coals and cook directly over them, fat side up to start. Pull at an internal 130–135°F for medium-rare and let it rest; carry-over will take it further. The grain inside a tri-tip changes direction about two thirds of the way along, so find the turn and change your knife angle with it — slicing the whole piece one way guarantees that half of it chews like rope.

If you have no red oak, use what burns clean and hot near you, and say so rather than pretending. The wood is regional, and that is the point of it.

sections.h: What this page could not settle
sections.text:
**Who named the cut.** Five claims, four decades, and no document this project has seen that settles it. The Santa Maria account is well attested as an account — Viegas telling it about Schutz — which is not the same as proof of first use.

**The 1978 registration.** Widely repeated in the trade, including the specific claim that the Chamber protected the whole menu rather than the meat. The Chamber's own explanation was unreachable from this machine on 16 September 2026 (HTTP 403), and no registration number has been checked here.

**What certification requires.** The association invites restaurants to get certified and lists certified locations; the criteria were not on the page this project read.

**What the valley drinks with it.** Nothing in the sources read here records a local convention. Anybody who has stood at a Santa Maria pit and watched what people poured knows more than this page does.
